doctrines/salvation/question: How is a human being saved — by grace, faith, works or the will — and will all be saved?
doctrines/salvation/summary: From Augustine and Pelagius to the Reformation, the Synod of Dort, Wesley, the New Perspective and Eastern theosis, Christians have agreed that salvation comes through Christ but disagreed sharply about how grace relates to human freedom, what justification is, what salvation finally consists in, and who will be saved.
doctrines/salvation/longText:
Every Christian tradition confesses that salvation is the gift of God in Jesus Christ. The disagreements concern how that gift reaches human beings and what it finally is. The early Greek fathers spoke chiefly of rescue from corruption and death and of growth into God (theosis): Irenaeus’ Christ "became what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself", and Athanasius’ Word "was made man that we might be made God". That vision still governs Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and Church of the East spirituality, refined by Maximus the Confessor and by Gregory Palamas’ distinction between God’s imparticipable essence and his participable energies.

In the Latin West the question became grace and free will. Pelagius, a British ascetic in Rome, insisted that God commands nothing impossible. Augustine, out of his own experience of a bound will, answered that since Adam humanity is a "mass of sin", that grace must heal and move the will from within, and that God freely predestines those he saves. Pelagianism was condemned (Carthage 418, Ephesus 431); the Gallic "semi-Pelagian" compromise of Cassian was answered at Orange (529) by a moderate Augustinianism without predestination to evil. Gottschalk’s ninth-century "twofold predestination", Thomas Aquinas’ synthesis of grace, merit and nature, and the Jesuit-Dominican conflict over Molina’s "middle knowledge" and Jansen’s Augustinus all reworked that inheritance.

The Reformation turned on justification. Luther, Melanchthon and Calvin taught that sinners are declared righteous before God for Christ’s sake through faith alone, his righteousness being "imputed" — though Luther’s "joyful exchange" and Calvin’s "mystical union" also put union with Christ at the centre. Trent (1547) answered that justification is both forgiveness and the inner renewal of the person by infused grace, with which the freed will cooperates. Within Protestantism the Remonstrants’ conditional election and resistible grace were rejected by the Synod of Dort (1618-19), whose canons later became the "five points of Calvinism"; Amyraldians, hyper-Calvinists and Wesleyan Arminians mapped further positions. Wesley’s doctrine of assurance and of entire sanctification fathered the Holiness movement, Keswick’s "higher life" and, through Holiness networks, Pentecostalism — which then divided over Durham’s "Finished Work".

Modern debates include free grace vs lordship salvation among evangelicals, the New Perspective on Paul (Sanders, Dunn, Wright) and its critics, the Lutheran-Catholic Joint Declaration (1999), and the long-running question of final destiny: eternal conscious punishment (the historic majority view), conditional immortality/annihilationism, and universal restoration from Origen and Gregory of Nyssa to modern "evangelical universalists". A featured comparison sets the "legal/forensic" and "relational/union" frameworks side by side.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/0/label: How is a human being saved — and what do grace, faith, works and the will each contribute?
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/0/text: Behind every soteriological debate sit linked questions: what went wrong with humanity, what God has done in Christ, how that reaches a person (grace, faith, sacraments, the will), what salvation finally is (pardon, healing, union, deification), and whether all will share in it.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/1/text: Justified "freely by his grace" (3:24) "by faith without the deeds of the law" (3:28); Abraham believed and it was counted to him (4:3); the Adam-Christ parallel (5:12-21). Central to Augustine, Luther, Calvin and the New Perspective alike.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/2/text: Foreknown, predestined, called, justified, glorified (8:29-30); Jacob loved and Esau hated, the potter and the clay (9:13-21); chosen "in him before the foundation of the world" (Eph 1:4). Read individually (Augustine, Calvin), corporately (many Arminians, Barth, New Perspective) or Christologically.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/3/label: James 2:14-26; Philippians 2:12-13 — faith, works and synergy
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/3/text: "By works a man is justified, and not by faith only" (Jas 2:24); "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God which worketh in you" (Phil 2:12-13). Key for Catholic, Orthodox, Arminian and lordship readings; harmonised by Protestants as evidence of living faith.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/4/label: 2 Peter 1:4; John 17:21-23; 2 Corinthians 3:18 — partakers of the divine nature
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/4/text: Believers become "partakers of the divine nature" and are "changed into the same image from glory to glory". The scriptural root of Eastern theosis and of Western "union with Christ" theologies.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/5/label: 1 Timothy 2:4; 1 Corinthians 15:22-28; Matthew 25:46 — all, and the end
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/5/text: God "will have all men to be saved"; "in Christ shall all be made alive … that God may be all in all"; yet "these shall go away into everlasting punishment". The texts at the heart of universalism, annihilationism and eternal conscious punishment.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/6/label: Irenaeus: he became what we are
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/6/text: Against the Gnostics Irenaeus describes salvation as Christ "recapitulating" Adam and leading humanity from infancy to maturity and incorruption — growth into God rather than escape from matter.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/7/label: Origen: the end is like the beginning
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/7/text: Free rational creatures fell from contemplation of God; through education and purifying punishment God will restore all, so that God is "all in all".
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/8/label: Athanasius: made man that we might be made God
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/8/text: The Word took flesh to undo corruption and death from within and to restore the image of God — the classic formula of theosis.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/9/text: Human nature, created good, retains the capacity to obey; grace is creation, law, Christ’s example and forgiveness.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/10/label: Augustine: grace heals a bound will
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/10/text: Since Adam all are fallen and the will cannot love God without inner, efficacious grace; God freely predestines the elect.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/11/label: Argument from infant baptism and the Lord’s Prayer
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/11/text: Augustine argues that the Church baptises infants "for the remission of sins" and that all pray "forgive us our debts" — so all inherit sin and all need grace. Pelagians replied that infants are baptised for the kingdom, not for guilt.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/12/label: Council of Carthage (418) and Pope Zosimus condemn Pelagianism
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/12/text: African bishops condemn denial of original sin and of grace as necessary for good works; Zosimus’ Tractoria follows; Ephesus (431) condemns Caelestius. Decision: Pelagianism rejected in East and West.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/13/label: Gallic monks: the first step can be ours
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/13/text: Cassian and later Faustus of Riez accept the need for grace but resist irresistible predestination: the initium fidei may arise from the will.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/14/label: Council of Orange (529): grace before faith, no predestination to evil
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/14/text: Caesarius’ council affirms that even the beginning of faith is grace, while anathematising predestination to evil. Approved by Boniface II (531).
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/15/text: The monk of Orbais teaches predestination of the reprobate to damnation; condemned at Mainz (848) and Quierzy (849) under Hincmar, then partly vindicated at Valence (855).
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/16/label: Maximus the Confessor: deification by grace
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/16/text: Maximus describes the whole economy as God becoming man so that man may become god by grace, through a human will freely conformed to the divine will in Christ.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/17/label: Aquinas: grace perfects nature, merit as gift
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/17/text: Habitual and actual grace, predestination as God’s gratuitous plan, merit as the fruit of grace; later Dominicans stress "physical premotion".
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/18/label: Palamas: participation in the uncreated energies
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/18/text: Hesychast saints really see the uncreated light; God is participated in his energies, not his essence. Decision: councils at Constantinople (1341-1351) endorse Palamas, canonised 1368.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/19/text: The sinner is declared righteous for Christ’s sake through faith alone; good works flow freely from faith but contribute nothing to justification.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/20/label: Erasmus vs Luther on free will (1524-25)
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/20/text: Erasmus pleads that Scripture’s commands and exhortations presuppose a will able to cooperate; Luther answers that commands show what we ought, not what we can, and that God’s foreknowledge binds the fallen will.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/21/label: Trent: justification as pardon and inner renewal
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/21/text: Justification is the remission of sins and the sanctification of the inner person by infused charity; it begins with prevenient grace and free cooperation, can increase, and can be lost by mortal sin.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/22/text: Thirty-three canons anathematise justification by faith alone understood as excluding cooperation, imputation without inner grace, and certainty of final perseverance. Decision: Western schism over justification confessionally fixed.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/23/label: Calvin and Dort: sovereign particular grace
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/23/text: Union with Christ by the Spirit yields the "double grace" of justification and sanctification; election is unconditional; Dort later codifies the five points.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/24/label: Arminius and the Remonstrants: resistible grace, conditional election
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/24/text: Prevenient grace enables all to believe; election is in Christ of those foreseen to believe; Christ died for all; grace can be resisted.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/25/text: An international Reformed synod rejects the Remonstrance; about 200 Remonstrant ministers are deposed and Oldenbarnevelt is executed (1619) in the accompanying political crisis.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/26/text: God’s knowledge of what free creatures would do reconciles efficacious providence with libertarian freedom; the papacy ends the De Auxiliis dispute (1607) without a verdict.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/27/label: Jansen and Port-Royal: Augustine’s grace revived
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/27/text: Augustinus (1640) teaches irresistible efficacious grace and a strict moral rigour; five propositions condemned by Innocent X (1653), Unigenitus (1713).
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/28/text: Prevenient grace for all, justification by faith with felt assurance, and entire sanctification as a second work of grace.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/29/text: A crisis of full surrender brings a life of victory by the indwelling Christ, counteracting rather than eradicating the sinful nature.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/30/label: Durham: the Finished Work of Calvary
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/30/text: Pentecostals divide between the holiness three-stage order and a two-stage order: sanctification is given at conversion and then appropriated.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/31/text: MacArthur argues saving faith includes submission to Christ as Lord; Hodges and Ryrie reply that this smuggles works into faith and destroys assurance.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/32/text: Sanders, Dunn and Wright argue that Paul’s target was ethnic boundary markers, not works-righteousness, and that justification concerns membership in God’s covenant people.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/33/text: From Origen and Gregory of Nyssa through Isaac of Nineveh and Julian of Norwich to modern evangelical universalists, a minority hopes that God’s love finally restores all.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/34/text: Justinian’s edict (543) and anathemas associated with the Second Council of Constantinople (553) condemn the pre-existence of souls and the restoration of demons and the damned; the conciliar status of the 15 anathemas is debated.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/35/text: Augustine’s defence of eternal conscious punishment becomes the Western consensus; from the 19th century, and widely after Fudge (1982) and Stott (1988), evangelical annihilationism revives.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/36/text: Justification and predestination become marks of rival confessions: Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic territories (Peace of Augsburg 1555), Remonstrant exile, Huguenot and Jansenist persecution.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/37/text: Wesley’s second blessing gives birth to Holiness denominations, which supply Pentecostalism’s first framework; the Finished Work dispute shapes the Assemblies of God (1914).
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/38/label: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999)
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/38/text: Lutherans and Catholics state a "consensus in basic truths": by grace alone, in faith in Christ’s saving work and not because of any merit, we are accepted by God; the mutual condemnations are said not to apply to the teaching as presented. Methodists (2006), Reformed (2017) and Anglicans (2016-17) later associate themselves.
doctrines/salvation/flow/nodes/39/text: Catholic and Orthodox churches teach grace-enabled synergy (Orthodox framed as theosis); Lutheran and Reformed churches forensic justification; Arminian-Wesleyan views dominate Methodist, Holiness and most Pentecostal churches (perhaps the majority of global evangelicals); a "new Calvinist" revival and the New Perspective debate continue; universalism and annihilationism are growing minority views among evangelicals.
